findings.title: P0-2 names manifest.sqlite3 as the reconciliation oracle but assigns no process to own the join
findings.quote: | P0-2 | **Coverage matrix** per account: area × (live count, downloaded, missing, bytes, last export); totals reconcile with manifest and disk | Answers "what is missing" without guessing from a global count | Matrix equals `manifest.sqlite3` summary and file counts for `example.harvest`; screenshot; test for a zero-download account |
findings.claim: Only Python opens manifest.sqlite3 today, and the web process is documented as the store's read-only consumer; the plan requires a three-way join (live counts in the socket store, downloaded/bytes in Python's manifest, file counts on disk) without saying which process performs it. The two halves already exist in the store: verify.compare() produces per-area live/exported/missing and handleVerifyResult stores it, and export totals carry per-area bytes. The acceptance wording therefore invites a second SQLite reader in the web process rather than reusing what the worker already sends.
findings.impact: Operator opens the coverage matrix during an export and gets numbers from a second reader over a commit-per-file, non-WAL SQLite file: stale rows or lock errors, and for a zero-download account (the plan's own test) a reader that creates an empty manifest makes the matrix silently show nothing. Node becomes co-owner of a schema Python writes.

findings.title: P0-4's per-file failure data needs a Python manifest migration the plan never names, and retry needs a per-key export mode
findings.quote: | P0-4 | **Download truth**: record per-file failures (path, reason, attempt) and surface "failed" separately from "missing"; retry a failure set | "Missing" currently conflates never-attempted and failed | Seeded fake failure renders; retry clears it; test |
findings.claim: The manifest schema has no reason or attempt column, and it is created with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so existing per-account databases get no new columns. A failure is written as status='failed', size 0, empty sha, with the traceback only in the worker log; needs() treats any status other than 'done' as re-download. 'Retry a failure set' also has no path: jobs carry only a mode (missing/force/...), so a retry re-enumerates and re-downloads the whole missing set. Both the record and the retry are Python-side; the plan states them as dashboard behaviour.
findings.impact: If implemented where the plan points, the web process alters a resume database it does not write, or failure reasons land in the JSON store while the manifest stays the source of truth, giving two answers to 'why is this missing'. Old exports keep the exact failed/never-attempted conflation P0-4 exists to remove, and 'retry a failure set' silently retries everything.

findings.title: store.flush() evicts still-running jobs once 1000 newer jobs exist, silently breaking the jobs view at the 500-account scale P0-3 targets
findings.claim: The cap is documented as 'completed jobs' but filters on nothing: it sorts every job by createdAt and replaces the in-memory map with the newest 1000. A 500-account run creates roughly one export job per account per wave plus an auto-scan job per completed export (handleExportDone -> startScan), so >1000 job records per cycle. A long-running wave-1 export created early can be evicted while still running; handleExportProgress and handleExportDone then call store.getJob(id) and return on null, so progress is dropped, release() never runs, and the account stays 'exporting'.
findings.impact: In a campaign-scale run, one or more finished exports never complete: the account shows 'exporting 0/0', the worker slot is never returned, and P0-1's 'durable list' quietly loses the row the operator needs. The failure is silent because every handler treats a missing job as 'not mine'.
findings.fix: Keep every active job (queued/running/twofa) regardless of the cap and apply the 1000 limit only to terminal jobs; never drop an id still present in pool.queue. A durable append-only job log would remove the cap question entirely.

findings.title: A restart rewrites running jobs to a terminal 'unknown' state the pool never requeues, so P0-1's retry is the only recovery
findings.claim: Store's constructor calls markStaleJobs() before WorkerPool is constructed, converting running/twofa jobs to 'unknown'. The pool's boot rebuild enqueues only 'queued' and requeues only 'running'; sweep() also examines only running/twofa. 'unknown' is therefore terminal: no queue, no pump, no requeue. store.test.mjs asserts this ('running jobs are marked unknown'), so it is intended behaviour with no recovery path.
findings.impact: After any deploy or crash during an export, that job appears as 'unknown - node restarted' forever and the account is forced to error/connected; nothing resumes it. A jobs view built on this data shows a terminal row whose only action is a retry the plan has not designed. The plan treats retry as a convenience; here it is the sole recovery for a known restart path.
findings.fix: Treat 'unknown' as queued in the pool boot (or let markStaleJobs leave the job 'queued' with an error note), so the existing requeue path resumes it; do this before P0-1 renders the state.

findings.title: P0-3's operator priority/order has no store field and no scheduler hook; a badge that nothing consumes will not change dispatch
findings.quote: | P0-3 | **Bulk queue + priority**: checkbox selection, export/recheck/scan selected, pin/reorder, priority badge, per-account note; state survives reload | 500-account campaign is one click per account today | 3 selected accounts produce 3 ordered jobs; order persists after restart; screenshot |
findings.claim: There is no per-account priority/order/note field: updateAccount copies a fixed whitelist, and accounts have no note (only legacy submissions do, via item.note). Dispatch order is computed from job type rank, notesMissing and job createdAt; waves enqueue every eligible account through fillWave. The only priority concepts are a hardcoded email list, an in-memory priorityDone Set and a payload.priority boolean. The plan also specifies selection persistence twice, in P0-3 (reload) and P1-2 (URL), with no owner.
findings.impact: Selecting and pinning three accounts produces three jobs in createdAt order, and the order resets on restart because the queue is rebuilt from rank/notesMissing/createdAt. The stated pain - a 500-account campaign managed one account at a time - survives, and the priority badge is decorative. If selection is kept in both the URL and server state, the two diverge on reload.
findings.fix: One owner per concept: priority/order/note as account fields written by a socket admin:priority event (extend updateAccount's whitelist) and consumed by queue.sort/enqueue/fillWave; selection lives only in the URL. Do not reuse the legacy item.note.

findings.title: flush() deletes jobs from the live map past 1000, including still-queued ones, and pump() silently drops their ids

With tied createdAt values the eviction is arbitrary, not oldest-first: a probe of 1005 creates in one tick evicted 5 jobs starting at index 70.

findings.title: 1000-job trim can evict a running job, drop its completion, and leak a worker slot at 500 accounts

Measured on this machine: 57 ms to build one account with 1,000 photos (1,000 OCR files, 1,000 thumbs; catalog JSON 940,298 bytes), i.e. 500 accounts at CONCURRENCY=4 = ~7.1 s per rebuild with S4 off, linear in total files, with no incremental path and no resumability. findings.impact: An operator leaves the Library tab open and roughly every two minutes the next poll blocks for seconds (7 s at 500 accounts; minutes with S4 on, PERF-2), serving stale counts and saturating the export tree's FS while other /api/admin requests queue behind it. P1-3 (global search) rides this same call, so its cost is the rebuild, not the query (query is 1 ms/165 rows, 328 ms/500k rows, PERF-11).
findings.fix: Serve the last good catalog and rebuild off the request path (invalidate -> background build, swap on resolve), raise TTL_MS above the measured rebuild time, and persist the catalog to a file the scanner updates so a restart does not pay a cold build.

findings.title: With S4 configured, one catalog rebuild issues 3 S3 HEADs per photo: 1.5 M HEADs and 4-65 minutes per 500-account rebuild

findings.claim: buildAccount calls s4Links per photo with src+thumbSrc+previewSrc(HEIC)+playSrc(video), and each entry is a serial-ish HEAD through a global 24-slot limiter (s4.js:90). Measured against a local S4 stub: 3,000 HEADs and 1,956 ms for one 1,000-HEIC account at 0 ms RTT, 31,422 ms at 30 ms RTT. Extrapolated to 500 accounts at CONCURRENCY=4: 1,500,000 HEADs, ~244 s per rebuild at 0 ms RTT, ~3,928 s (65 min) at 30 ms RTT. findings.claim: The client always requests the whole area in one response, and the server honours it (`everything` -> slice = all, export.js:350-357) after doing per-item fs.stat work for every row. Measured: 142 items = 60,461 bytes (426 B/item), 6.8 ms warm / 9.5 ms cold of server work; 1,000 items = ~426 KB, ~35-45 ms of stats. Every response carries `cache-control: no-store` (api.js:376), and there is no compression middleware in server/app.js and no nginx gzip config in the repo, so each area switch, filter keystroke (250 ms debounce) and 30 s export tick re-transfers the full payload.
findings.impact: At 1k photos the operator pays ~426 KB per filter change over the wire (0.7 s on a 5 Mbit link) plus a 1,000-tile React render; at 5k - the size FEATURES itself names - it is ~2.1 MB per keystroke pause.
findings.fix: Set PAGE_SIZE to 120-200 and use the existing page/pages response (the server already paginates), send a slim item (drop src/previewSrc/playSrc from the list), and add `compression()` or a per-account ETag with a short max-age.

findings.title: pump() recounts running exports inside the queue loop: O(queue x jobs) per call, 2-6 ms each, ~1 s per 500-account enqueue storm
findings.quote: const running = [...this.store.jobs.values()].filter(
findings.claim: For every queued export/import entry the pump rebuilds an array of all jobs to count the running ones, so one pass over the queue costs queue_length x jobs_map_size. Measured with 984 queued exports and 1,000 jobs: 984,000 filter iterations, 6 ms on the first call and 2.14 ms steady state per pump. pump() runs on every enqueue and every release (worker-pool.js:751, 890), so queueing 500 accounts adds ~500 x ~0.5-1 ms of synchronous work, and pump also calls sweep() (a full 1,000-job scan) first.
findings.impact: A 500-account bulk queue blocks the socket event loop for roughly a second across the enqueues - the same loop that broadcasts admin:account and answers every dashboard ack, so the panel stutters exactly when the operator bulk-queues.
findings.fix: Count running exports once before the for-loop (and once before sweep), and keep a running counter maintained on dispatch/release instead of recomputing from the map.

findings.title: Every store mutation rewrites the entire store file synchronously: 3.1 ms and 1.68 MB per flush at 500 accounts + 1,000 jobs
findings.quote: fs.writeFileSync(
findings.claim: scheduleSave() coalesces to one write per 120 ms, and each flush JSON.stringifies and writeFileSyncs items+accounts+jobs in full. Measured with 500 synthetic accounts (real field shape and sizes) and 1,000 jobs: 3.1 ms per flush and a 1,684,171-byte file. During parallel exports the account updates arrive up to 16/s (one per exporting worker, exporter.py progress throttle 1.0 s), i.e. the 8 writes/s ceiling = ~25 ms/s of synchronous stringify+write (~13 MB/s of disk) on the socket event loop, growing linearly with account count.
findings.impact: At 500 accounts the dashboard's own data source costs ~2.5% of the socket loop continuously while exporting; at 5,000 accounts the same code writes ~17 MB eight times a second and the store file becomes the write-amplification tail of the whole panel.
findings.fix: Persist per-account files (or append-only journal) and flush only dirty records; keep the full rewrite on a longer cadence (e.g. 5 s) or on shutdown.

findings.title: admin:account pushes the full account object (945 B median, 3.3 KB max) and the client maps a 1,000-row array on each event
findings.quote: nsp.emit("admin:account", {
findings.claim: Every store 'account' mutation - and each exporting worker produces one per second - broadcasts the whole account (adminAccount returns `{...account}`, store.js:482, including password, sessionDir, identity, counts, export.areas) to every admin socket. Measured event payload: 1,617 bytes including stats; accounts are 945 B median, 3,296 B max. The client replaces the row by `.map()` over the entire account array (up to accountPageSize 1000, useAdminSocket.js:26/204) and re-renders the list. 16 exporting workers = 16 events/s = 16 full-list reconciliations/s of up to 1,000 rows.
findings.impact: While exports run, the accounts list repaints ~16x/s over up to 1,000 rows (a full array copy plus React diff each time) and receives ~26 KB/s of mostly-irrelevant account bodies per open panel - visible jank on the list the operator is trying to click.
findings.fix: Push a compact row ({id,status,export:{done,total,phase},badges,countsUpdatedAt}); keep the full object behind admin:account (on-demand). On the client, keep accounts in a Map keyed by id and patch one entry.

findings.title: Gallery stats each item's thumb/preview/play twice: 3 redundant fs.stat per tile, 3,000 extra syscalls per 1k page
findings.quote: preview: await previewFor(root, item.path),
findings.claim: The object literal already resolves thumbFor/previewFor/playFor (lines 361-368), then line 373 calls previewFor and playFor again inside the s4Links argument list, and s4Links itself stats nothing but receives the already-known `cached` thumb. Per item that is 3 extra fs.stat calls (2 in the literal, 3 repeated) plus one fileExists for OCR, so a 1,000-item page issues ~3,000 avoidable stat syscalls (~10 ms) and doubles the syscall count of the listing itself.
findings.impact: Small but pure waste on the hottest listing path, and it hides the real per-item cost (7-8 syscalls/tile) from anyone profiling the 1k case.
findings.fix: Hoist the three results into consts (thumb/preview/play) before the object literal and pass those into s4Links.

findings.title: P1-4 clustering is cheap only if done per account first: a global dedupeSeeds over raw findings is 242 ms at 45k rows
findings.quote: if (file && !current.files.includes(file)) current.files.push(file);
findings.claim: dedupeSeeds checks `files.includes` per duplicate, so a phrase present in every account costs O(n) per merge: measured 242 ms to dedupe 45,000 synthetic findings (500 accounts x 90) and 54 ms of that is isSpamPhrase. Deduping per account first (95 ms measured for 500 calls) and then grouping by normalizePhrase is ~0 ms (84 clusters), i.e. the cross-account step the plan asks for is free and the O(n^2) merge is avoidable.
findings.impact: A naive implementation rebuilds the 242 ms dedupe on every seed view; the catalog path (per-account dedupe at build time + a Map group) is 3x cheaper and constant per request.
findings.fix: Cluster over catalog.seeds (already deduped per account at build time); use a Set for `files` if dedupeSeeds itself must handle cross-account input.

findings.title: Listing caches are per-path and never evict: memory grows with total files, ~45 MB at 500 x 1k photos
findings.quote: dirCache.set(real, { at: Date.now(), mtimeMs: stat.mtimeMs, entries });
findings.claim: dirCache/driveCache/jsonCache are module-level Maps keyed by absolute path with no size bound and no eviction (the 60 s check is only on read, so a stale entry lives forever). Each cached listing holds one object per file ({name,size,mtime} ~90 B). At 500 accounts x 1,000 photos that is ~500,000 retained entries (~45 MB) plus one array per directory, never released, in the web process that also runs the catalog (504 MB RSS at 500k catalog rows, PERF-11).
findings.impact: Memory grows with the campaign's total file count, not with visitors, and no restart happens mid-campaign: the panel's resident set creeps to hundreds of MB and then holds, on a host also running 16 export workers.
findings.fix: Bound dirCache with a small LRU (e.g. 256 dirs) or key it by account and drop on invalidation; same for s4.js `seen` (which clears at 20k, PERF-2).
